beginner: Mulberry is about as easygoing as a fruit tree gets when it comes to soil. It does best in a deep, rich, well-drained loam, but it also grows in sandy soil and even heavy clay, and it puts up with poor, dry ground once it is established. The one thing it does not want is soil that stays wet: constant waterlogging can rot the roots. Full sun and any soil that drains is really all it asks, and a little compost worked in at planting gives a young tree a good start.
seasoned: Mulberry is broadly soil-tolerant. It grows best in a deep, moist, well-drained loam but performs across sandy loams, sands, and clays, and tolerates infertile, dry, and even mildly alkaline ground once established (white mulberry in particular takes a wide pH span). The only real limit is drainage: chronically waterlogged soil invites root rot. Site it in full sun on any freely draining ground; a modest amount of organic matter at planting speeds establishment, but rich soil is not required and heavy feeding is unnecessary.

beginner: Mulberry grows well across a wide range of soil pH and is not fussy (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). It is happiest around pH 6.0 to 7.0 but tolerates soil from about 5.5 up to 8.0, including the mildly alkaline soils that trouble many fruit trees. For most gardens you do not need to adjust the pH at all; just make sure the soil drains.
seasoned: Mulberry is pH-adaptable, doing best around pH 6.0 to 7.0 but tolerating roughly 5.5 to 8.0. White mulberry in particular handles alkaline ground that stresses many stone fruits, so pH correction is rarely needed. Test before planting if in doubt, but in most soils the practical limits are drainage and sun, not pH.

beginner: Mulberry hardly ever needs feeding. It is a fast, vigorous tree that does fine on its own in most soils. If a young tree looks weak or the leaves are pale, scatter a little balanced fertilizer around the root zone in early spring and water it in. Do not overdo it, especially with nitrogen (the first number on the bag), because too much just makes leafy growth instead of fruit. Do not feed late in the year.
seasoned: Mulberry is a vigorous, undemanding tree that rarely needs feeding once established; on decent soil it grows fast on its own. If a young tree is weak or the leaves pale, apply a light broadcast of balanced fertilizer around the root zone in early spring and water it in. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which pushes rank, soft growth at the expense of fruit and can worsen bird-magnet leafiness. Never feed late in the season.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) covers the rare time a mulberry needs feeding. Most mature trees need none at all. When in doubt, feed less, because too much nitrogen means leaves instead of fruit.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 is more than enough for the rare occasion a mulberry needs feeding. Mature trees typically need nothing; err on the side of underfeeding, since excess nitrogen (N) drives vegetative growth over fruit.

beginner: If a young tree needs a boost, use about 1/2 to 1 cup of 10-10-10 for each year of its age, spread around the roots in early spring and watered in. A grown, healthy tree usually needs no fertilizer at all. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole; wait until the tree starts growing.
seasoned: If feeding a young or weak tree, roughly 1/2 to 1 cup of 10-10-10 per year of tree age in early spring is ample, broadcast around the root zone and watered in, up to a few cups for a larger tree. Established trees on reasonable soil generally need no fertilizer at all. Do not fertilize in the planting hole; wait until growth begins.

beginner: Mulberry is self-fruitful, which means one named tree makes fruit on its own with no second tree needed (a few wild seedlings are single-sex, so buy a named fruiting variety and this never comes up). Because it is a big, fast tree, the things that matter are not vegetable-garden pairings but where you put it: keep grass and weeds pulled back from a young trunk so it establishes faster, and above all keep it away from paths, patios, driveways, and parked cars, because the dropped fruit stains everything it lands on. Under the dense canopy, lawn and most plants struggle from shade and shallow roots, so plan for mulch or shade-tolerant groundcover there.
seasoned: Mulberry is self-fruitful, so a single named tree fruits on its own without a pollinizer (a few wild seedlings are dioecious, but named cultivars sidestep that). The interactions that matter are about siting a large, vigorous tree, not classic vegetable companions: clear turf back from a young trunk to speed establishment, and site the tree well away from walkways, patios, driveways, and parking, since the abundant dropped fruit stains hard surfaces and gets tracked indoors. The dense canopy and shallow feeder roots make the ground beneath it a tough spot for lawn or bedding plants, so mulch it or use a shade-tolerant groundcover.

beginner: Birds strip the ripe berries fast. You will see missing fruit, half-eaten berries, and purple bird droppings under and around the tree. Big flocks can show up daily while the fruit ripens.
seasoned: Ripe and near-ripe berries disappear, half-eaten fruit and purple droppings appear on the ground and on nearby surfaces, and flocks work the tree through the ripening weeks. On a large tree the loss is simply shared; on a small or netted tree it can be nearly total if not managed.

beginner: Lots of birds love sweet, soft mulberries and eat them as they ripen. This is the main reason people lose fruit to the tree, though it is also why a mulberry is such a great tree for attracting birds.
seasoned: Many birds, especially catbirds, mockingbirds, robins, and waxwings, are drawn to sweet, soft mulberries and feed heavily as they ripen. This is the number-one reason home growers lose fruit, and it is a feature as much as a pest, since a mulberry is one of the best wildlife trees you can plant.

beginner: For a small tree, cover it with bird netting when the first berries start to color, and pick ripe fruit every day so there is less left for the birds. A big tree is too large to net, so the usual approach is to accept that you are sharing, or even to let the mulberry act as a decoy that keeps birds off your other fruit.
seasoned: For a small tree, drape bird netting over it as the first berries color, and harvest ripe fruit promptly each day so less hangs available. For a large tree, netting is impractical; the traditional answer is to plant enough that there is plenty to share, and some growers deliberately keep a mulberry as a decoy to lure birds away from cherries and other prized fruit.

beginner: You cannot really keep birds off a big mulberry, so plan on sharing; luckily the tree makes far more fruit than you can eat. Only bother netting small or dwarf trees, and pick ripe fruit quickly.
seasoned: There is no way to keep birds off a large mulberry, so plan the siting and the crop around sharing: a big tree yields far more than a household can use. Net only small or dwarf trees, and pick promptly.

beginner: Tiny white flies rise up off the undersides of the leaves when you brush the branches, sometimes leaving a sticky film and black sooty mold below. They rarely bother an established tree much.
seasoned: Tiny white flying insects lift off the undersides of leaves when disturbed, sometimes with sticky honeydew and sooty mold on lower foliage in a heavy infestation. Vigor is rarely affected on an established tree.

beginner: Whiteflies are small sap-sucking insects that gather under the leaves. They show up on mulberry fairly often but rarely do real harm.
seasoned: Whiteflies (including the mulberry whitefly) are sap-feeders that colonize leaf undersides. They are a common but minor mulberry pest and mostly a cosmetic nuisance.

beginner: A healthy tree does not need treatment. On a small tree with a lot of them, spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water or insecticidal soap, and welcome the ladybugs and lacewings that eat them.
seasoned: A healthy tree needs no treatment. If numbers are high on a small tree, a strong water spray to the leaf undersides or an insecticidal-soap application knocks them back; encourage the lacewings and ladybugs that prey on them.

beginner: Keep the tree healthy and go easy on nitrogen feeding, which draws whiteflies. Natural predators usually keep them under control outside.
seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and avoid heavy nitrogen feeding, which encourages the soft growth whiteflies favor. Natural predators usually keep them in balance outdoors.

beginner: Small holes, sawdust-like frass, or oozing on the trunk or big branches, mostly on trees that are already stressed or damaged. A healthy tree is rarely bothered.
seasoned: Small entry holes, frass, or oozing on the trunk and larger limbs, usually on trees already stressed by drought, injury, or decline. Healthy, vigorous mulberries are seldom attacked.

beginner: A few kinds of borer (beetle and moth larvae) can get into mulberry, but usually only when the tree is already weak from drought, wounds, or old age. They tend to follow trouble rather than start it.
seasoned: Several wood-boring beetle and moth larvae can attack mulberry, but almost always as a secondary problem on trees weakened by drought stress, mechanical wounds, or age. Borers follow decline rather than cause it in a healthy tree.

beginner: The best fix is a healthy tree: water it in droughts, keep mowers and trimmers off the trunk, and cut out and destroy any dead or infested branches. Once larvae are inside the wood, no spray reaches them.
seasoned: The durable control is tree health: water through droughts, avoid trunk wounds from mowers and trimmers, and prune out and destroy any dead or infested wood. There is no practical rescue spray for larvae already tunneling inside.

beginner: Keep the tree healthy and avoid wounding the trunk. A well-placed, watered mulberry rarely has borer trouble.
seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and unwounded. A well-sited, adequately watered mulberry rarely gives borers an opening.

beginner: Some berries grow oddly, with the little segments puffing up hard and greenish so the fruit looks like tiny popcorn instead of a soft berry. Those berries never ripen right and hang on the tree.
seasoned: Some berries on the tree swell up abnormally, with individual segments (carpels) enlarging and staying hard and greenish, so the fruit looks like a little cluster of popcorn kernels instead of a normal soft berry. Affected fruit does not ripen properly and clings to the tree.

beginner: Popcorn disease is a fungus (Ciboria carunculoides) that gets into the developing fruit and makes it swell into hard, popcorn-like lumps. It mostly shows up in the South, and white mulberries and hybrids catch it most. It is usually minor but can cost you fruit on a tree you grow for eating.
seasoned: Popcorn disease is caused by the fungus Ciboria carunculoides, which infects the developing fruit and turns the carpels into hard sclerotia. It is largely a southern problem, and white mulberries and their hybrids are the most susceptible; it is usually of minor importance but can cause real fruit loss on trees grown for eating.

beginner: No home spray fixes it. The control is cleanup: pick off and throw away the affected berries, and rake up and bury or bin the fallen fruit under the tree, because that is where the fungus waits out the winter to come back next year.
seasoned: There is no home spray that cures it. Control is sanitation: as the disease appears, remove and destroy the affected fruit on the tree and rake up and bury or discard fallen fruit and debris beneath it, since that is where the fungus overwinters to reinfect next year.

beginner: Keep the ground under the tree clean of fallen fruit each year so the fungus cannot overwinter. If popcorn disease is common in your area, choose a red mulberry or a tougher hybrid rather than the most susceptible white types.
seasoned: Year-round sanitation is the prevention: clear fallen and mummified fruit each season so the fungus has nowhere to overwinter. Where popcorn disease is a known local problem, favor red mulberry or a more resistant hybrid over the most susceptible white types.

beginner: Leaves get angular, water-soaked spots that turn dark, and new shoots can have black streaks; bad cases kill the shoot tips. It usually just looks bad rather than harming an established tree, and it is worst in wet weather.
seasoned: Angular, water-soaked spots appear on the leaves and turn dark, and young shoots can show black streaks or stripes; badly hit shoot tips may die back. Damage is usually cosmetic on an established tree and worst in wet springs.

beginner: Bacterial blight is a bacterium (Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori) that spreads in cool, wet spring weather and infects new growth. It is a minor disease that shows up in wet years and rarely hurts a healthy tree.
seasoned: Bacterial blight is caused by the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori, which spreads in cool, wet spring weather and enters young tissue. It is a minor mulberry disease that flares in wet seasons and rarely threatens a healthy tree.

beginner: Cut out and throw away the blackened, blighted shoots in dry weather, and avoid watering over the top of the tree so the leaves stay drier. On a backyard tree, that cleanup is all that is needed.
seasoned: Prune out and destroy blackened, blighted shoots during dry weather to remove the bacterial source, and avoid overhead watering that keeps foliage wet. No spray is warranted on a home tree beyond this sanitation.

beginner: Keep the tree open so air moves through it, prune only when it is dry, and remove any infected shoots. A healthy, well-spaced tree easily shrugs this off most years.
seasoned: Keep the canopy open and the foliage dry, prune only in dry weather, and remove infected wood promptly. A vigorous, well-spaced tree shrugs off the disease in most years.

beginner: Spots on the leaves, or whitish patches underneath them in late summer, sometimes with a few leaves dropping in a wet year. It rarely affects how the tree grows or fruits.
seasoned: Scattered fungal leaf spots, or whitish patches (false mildew and powdery mildew) on leaf undersides in mid to late summer, sometimes with modest leaf drop on older trees in a wet season. Vigor and cropping are rarely affected.

beginner: A few minor leaf fungi (leaf spots and mildews) can mark mulberry leaves, mostly late in the season and in wet weather. On mulberry they are just cosmetic and rarely worth doing anything about.
seasoned: A group of minor leaf fungi (Cercospora and Cercosporella leaf spots, false mildew, and powdery mildews) can spot or coat mulberry foliage, mostly late in the season and mostly in wet weather. On mulberry these are cosmetic and seldom worth treating.

beginner: A healthy tree needs no treatment. Rake up and remove fallen leaves in fall to cut down on next year's spores, and keep the tree open so air flows through. Sprays are only for special trees with a bad, repeated problem.
seasoned: No treatment is needed on a healthy tree. Rake and remove fallen leaves in autumn to reduce carryover, and keep the canopy open for airflow. Fungicides are reserved for prized specimens with a serious recurring problem.

beginner: Keeping the tree open, cleaning up fallen leaves in fall, and letting air move through are all you need. A well-grown mulberry carries these without real harm.
seasoned: Open-canopy pruning, autumn leaf cleanup, and good air movement are the whole prevention program. Well-grown mulberries carry these diseases without meaningful harm.

beginner: Water a new mulberry regularly for its first year or two, about once a week when it does not rain, so the roots get going. After that it is very drought-tolerant and an older tree seldom needs watering, though a good soak while the berries are filling makes them bigger and sweeter. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs almost none.
seasoned: Water regularly through the first one to two seasons to establish the roots, roughly weekly in the absence of rain. After that, mulberry is notably drought-tolerant and an established tree rarely needs irrigation, though watering through the final weeks of fruit sizing improves size and sweetness. Cut back sharply in winter dormancy.

beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches down to the roots, not just a splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak. An older tree needs little, but a deep weekly soak while the fruit is filling, if the weather is dry, pays off in better berries. Deep soaks grow deep, drought-proof roots.
seasoned: Water deeply each time so moisture reaches the full root depth rather than wetting only the surface. For an establishing tree, on the order of 5 gallons per soak; a bearing tree that is watered at all wants the rough equivalent of an inch per week during fruit fill in dry spells. Deep, infrequent soaks build the deep roots that carry mulberry through drought.

beginner: Water the ground around the roots with a drip line, soaker hose, or a slow trickle from a hose, spreading it out toward the edge of the branches. The main thing is that the soil drains between waterings; mulberry hates sitting in water much more than it minds being dry.
seasoned: Water at the root zone by drip, soaker, or a slow hose out toward the drip line, keeping the trunk base itself uncrowded. Overhead watering is not the concern it is with stone fruit, but soil that drains freely between waterings matters most, since mulberry dislikes standing water far more than dryness.

beginner: Too much water, or soil that stays soggy, shows up as yellow leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree that just sits there or goes downhill. Since mulberry handles dry soil so well, staying too wet is the bigger risk. Soil that never dries out is your cue to back off.
seasoned: Overwatering or poor drainage shows as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists in wet soil, and a stalled or declining tree, since waterlogged roots suffocate. Because mulberry is so drought-adapted, chronic wet feet is a far more common cause of trouble than dryness; soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign.

beginner: Too little water shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, and some early leaf drop in a long dry spell, and smaller berries if it runs dry while the fruit is filling. An established mulberry shrugs off dry spells and usually bounces back; the tree itself is rarely killed by drought.
seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, and early leaf drop in a prolonged drought, and on the fruit as poor sizing during the fill period. An established mulberry tolerates real dry stress and usually recovers, but berries sized under drought stay small; the tree itself is rarely lost to dryness.

beginner: While the tree is settling in, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps it grow the deep roots that make it so drought-tough later.
seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil evenly moist, never waterlogged. A deep soak of about 5 gallons weekly, adjusted for rain and heat, builds the deep root system mulberry relies on to shrug off later droughts.

beginner: While the berries are filling, an older tree in a dry spell does better with about an inch of water a week as deep soaks. Steady water now means bigger, sweeter fruit. If it is raining regularly, you do not need to add any.
seasoned: During fruit fill, a bearing tree in a dry spell benefits from the equivalent of about an inch of water per week as deep soaks. Steady moisture now translates into larger, sweeter berries; an established tree with regular rain needs nothing extra.

beginner: After the leaves drop and the tree is resting for winter, it needs almost no water. Let rain do the work and water only during a long dry winter stretch. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.
seasoned: Once the tree is dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely on rainfall and water only in a prolonged dry winter. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.

beginner: Give a deep soak now and then at the ground rather than a little every day, and make sure the soil drains between waterings. Mulberry handles dry soil far better than wet. Young trees need steady water for the first year or two to get established; after that, an older tree can often go without watering entirely.
seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone to encourage deep rooting; free drainage between waterings matters more than frequency, since mulberry is drought-adapted but intolerant of standing water. Young trees need consistent moisture through their first season or two to establish; mature trees are strongly drought-tolerant and often need no irrigation at all.

seasoned: The one window where watering clearly pays off is fruit fill, the couple of weeks as berries size and sweeten; a bearing tree kept watered then, in a dry spell, sizes better fruit. Establishment (the first season or two) is the other sensitive period. Outside those, an established mulberry is remarkably self-sufficient.

beginner: Mulberries do not keep on the counter. Ripe fruit gets soft and starts to spoil within a day, so eat them the day you pick them or put them in the fridge right away. They stain everything, so work over a bowl.
seasoned: Mulberries are extremely perishable and do not hold at room temperature; ripe fruit begins to soften and ferment within a day. Eat them the day they are picked, or refrigerate immediately. They also stain hands, cloth, and counters, so handle over a bowl.

beginner: Keep ripe mulberries in the fridge, unwashed, in a shallow open container, and eat them within 2 to 3 days (wash them only right before eating). They spoil fast and bruise easily, which is why you almost never see them in a grocery store; a mulberry is a fruit you grow or pick yourself.
seasoned: Refrigerate ripe mulberries unwashed in a shallow, breathable container and use within 2 to 3 days; washing before storage hastens breakdown. Their very short shelf life (and how poorly they pack and ship) is exactly why mulberries are a home-grown and farmers-market fruit, rarely a grocery one.

beginner: Mulberries freeze really well, which is the best way to deal with a big crop. Rinse them gently, drain and pat dry, spread them on a tray to freeze, then pack them into freezer bags. They keep for months and are great for baking, jam, syrup, and smoothies.
seasoned: Mulberries freeze very well. Rinse gently, drain and pat dry, freeze in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to freezer bags. Frozen berries keep for many months and are excellent for baking, jam, syrup, and smoothies. Freezing is the practical way to handle a heavy crop that ripens faster than you can eat it fresh.

beginner: Ripe mulberries only last a couple of days and stain easily, so have a plan for them: pick into shallow containers, chill or freeze them right away, and turn a big pick into jam, syrup, or frozen bags instead of letting them drop and stain the ground.
seasoned: Because tree-ripe mulberries last only days and stain readily, plan for the crop: pick into shallow containers, refrigerate or freeze promptly, and turn a heavy flush into jam, syrup, or the freezer rather than letting it drop and stain the ground.

beginner: Pick a mulberry first by your climate and how big a tree you want, then by the fruit. For cold winters, choose a hardy hybrid like Illinois Everbearing or Silk Hope; for warm areas, low-chill types like Pakistan, Black Beauty, or Oscar do great. For a small yard or a pot, choose a real dwarf like Dwarf Everbearing. Almost all named fruiting varieties fruit on their own, so one tree is enough. The one rule is to buy a NAMED fruiting variety, not an unnamed seedling, because a few wild seedlings turn out to be male and never fruit.
seasoned: Choose a mulberry first by climate and size, then by fruit. For cold winters, pick a hardy hybrid such as Illinois Everbearing or Silk Hope (zones 4 to 5 and up); for mild and warm regions, low-chill types like Pakistan, Black Beauty, and Oscar shine. For a small space or a container, choose a genuine dwarf such as Dwarf Everbearing. Nearly all named fruiting cultivars are self-fruitful and often parthenocarpic, so a single tree bears; the caveat is to buy a NAMED fruiting cultivar rather than an unnamed seedling, since a few wild seedlings are single-sex.

beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to outdoors) does not apply to mulberry. You plant it as a dormant bare-root tree in late winter or early spring, or from a pot, so there is no tender young plant to ease outdoors.
seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to mulberry. It is planted as a dormant bare-root tree in late winter to early spring, or as a container tree, not raised from a tender indoor seedling, so there is no soft transplant to acclimate.

beginner: Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter to early spring, before the buds open, once the ground can be dug; a potted tree can go in during the growing season if you keep it watered. Soak bare roots in water for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots out, and set the tree at the same depth it grew before (if it is a grafted tree, keep the graft bump above the soil). Fill in with the soil you dug out, water it in well, and keep the area around it weed-free and mulched. Give it plenty of space, because a standard mulberry gets big.
seasoned: Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter to early spring before bud break, once the ground can be worked; container trees can go in through the growing season with attentive watering. Soak bare roots for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them and set the tree at the depth it grew in the nursery; if it is grafted, keep the graft union above the soil line. Backfill with native soil, water in well, and keep the surrounding area weed-free and mulched. Give it room: a standard mulberry is a large, spreading tree.

beginner: If you grow a dwarf mulberry in a pot, use a chunky, free-draining mix made for shrubs and trees, not a soft peaty potting soil that stays soggy. A bark-based mix with perlite or pumice drains well. Do not use soil dug from the yard in a pot, because it packs down and drains poorly when watered often.
seasoned: For a dwarf or weeping mulberry in a container, use a coarse, free-draining soilless mix built for woody plants, not a peat-heavy potting soil. A bark-based mix (composted pine bark with perlite or pumice) gives the air-filled porosity roots need; skip native garden soil, which compacts under frequent irrigation.

seasoned: Keep amendments drainage-first: blend in extra perlite or pumice if the base mix is water-retentive, and top-dress with a thin compost layer rather than mixing heavy organics throughout. Avoid moisture-retentive additives, which work against the freely draining root zone mulberry wants.

beginner: A potted mulberry dries out much faster than one in the ground, so check it often in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until water runs out the bottom. It still hates sitting in water, so never leave the pot in a full saucer. In winter, when the tree is resting, give just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
seasoned: A potted mulberry dries far faster than one in the ground and has no deep soil to draw on, so check moisture often in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until it runs from the drainage holes. It still resents standing water, so never leave the pot in a full saucer. Through dormancy it needs only enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.

seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, so feed lightly and often rather than in one heavy dose: a dilute balanced liquid feed every few weeks through the spring-to-midsummer flush, then stop by late summer so no soft growth is pushed into frost. Do not feed at planting, and ease off once the tree goes dormant.

beginner: Roots in a pot get much colder than roots in the ground, because cold reaches the soil from every side. A mulberry that is hardy in your yard can still have its roots freeze in a pot. Before hard freezes, either sink the pot to its rim in a garden bed or move it into an unheated but sheltered spot like a garage or shed that stays cold but not deep-freezing. It still needs the cold to rest, so do not bring it into a warm room.
seasoned: Roots in a container sit several zones colder than roots in the ground, so a mulberry hardy in your soil may still freeze its roots in a pot. Before hard freezes, sink the pot to its rim in a bed or move it to an unheated but sheltered space (garage or shed) that holds dormancy without the deep lows that kill exposed roots. It still needs its winter chill, so do not overwinter it in a heated room.

beginner: A standard mulberry is far too large and vigorous for a pot, so container growing means choosing a naturally dwarf or weeping variety like Dwarf Everbearing, which is bred for it and even fruits young in a pot. In a big, well-draining container it can be a productive patio tree, but plan on regular watering, occasional root pruning, and winter protection of the pot. For the everyday full-size mulberry, plant it in the ground.
seasoned: A standard mulberry is far too large and vigorous for containers, so container culture means starting with a genetic-dwarf or weeping cultivar (Dwarf Everbearing and similar), which are bred for pots and bear young. Given the largest practical, freely draining pot, such a tree makes a productive patio specimen, but expect regular watering, periodic root pruning to hold size, and winter root protection. For the ordinary full-size mulberry, in-ground is the only sensible choice.

beginner: A self-watering pot (one with a water tank in the bottom) is not a good choice for mulberry. The tank keeps the lower roots wet all the time, and wet roots are the one thing mulberry really dislikes. Use a pot that drains freely and let the soil dry out a bit between waterings.
seasoned: A self-watering or sub-irrigated planter is a poor match for mulberry. Its reservoir keeps the lower root zone continuously moist, and mulberry's one real intolerance is standing water at the roots. Use a pot that drains freely and let the mix dry between waterings, rather than a constant water table held against the roots.

In exposed spots wrap or shade the lower trunk, and pile mulch around a sunk pot to insulate the roots. You want a cold, steady rest without the deep freezes that kill exposed roots, and be careful that a too-warm spot can wake the tree early.
seasoned: Cold protection in a pot covers more than the roots: an exposed trunk and, on a grafted tree, the graft union are also vulnerable to freeze. Wrap or shade the lower trunk in exposed sites and bank mulch or sink the pot to insulate the roots. Aim for a cold, stable dormancy without the deep lows that kill exposed roots; a too-warm shelter that breaks dormancy early is its own hazard.

beginner: You do not rotate a mulberry the way you rotate vegetables, because it stays put for decades. Unlike peaches, mulberry has no special replant problem, so it can follow most things. The main thing is to pick the right spot from the start, away from paths and patios, because a big tree is hard to move.
